warmup.q: A payments program adds the record of an approved payment to its log file with write(), the call that writes bytes to a file. The call returns success, and the program tells the card reader "approved". The power goes out two seconds later. Is the record in the file after the restart?
options: Probably not: it was most likely still only in RAM
Yes: the file system's journal, its log of its own changes, protects it
Only if the file was opened for adding to the end (O_APPEND)
warmup.why: write() copies the bytes into the page cache, the kernel's copy of files in RAM, and returns. The kernel writes them to the disk about 30 seconds later, or when the program calls fsync. A journal (ext4's, by default) keeps the file system's own records of names and sizes in order after a crash. It doesn't make data safe that nobody fsynced. O_APPEND only decides where in the file the bytes go. The first option is the trap, because everything a program can see says the write happened.

sections.h: The page cache: why the second read of a file is fast
sections.html:
cat is a command that reads a file and prints it. In the lab box, it reads a 512 MB file in 1.0 s the first time, and in 0.16 s the second. Nothing about cat changed between the runs. The second time, every page of the file was already in RAM.

Storage is slow next to memory. A read from an SSD (the kind of disk most computers have now, built from chips that keep data without power) takes around 0.1 ms. Copying the same 4 KB within RAM takes about a microsecond. And programs read the same data over and over. Java opens the same library files every time it starts. A program that answers requests reads the same settings file for each one. And Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages, hands out a message seconds after it wrote it.

The simplest fix is for each program to keep its own copy of what it reads: a cache. It falls short fast. Ten programs reading one file keep ten copies. The cache dies with its program, so a restarted program starts cold. And a program caching a file can't know when another program changes it.

So the kernel, the core of the operating system, keeps one cache of file pages for the whole machine: the page cache. A page is the 4 KB unit the kernel handles memory in. Every read(), the system call (a request to the kernel) that a program uses to read a file, goes through the page cache. On a miss, when the page isn't there yet, the kernel reads it from storage into a free frame, a 4 KB piece of RAM. It keeps the page there, and copies the bytes into the program's own memory. On a hit, it only copies. When it sees a file being read in order, it reads ahead: it fetches the next pages before the program asks. And mmap of a file (Copy-on-write, mmap and the OOM killer) maps these same frames into a program's memory, so a mapped file and a read() of it share one copy.

The page cache lives in RAM that nobody else is using. In one run in the lab box, free -m, a command that shows memory in MB, showed 3,120 MB of buff/cache, only 4,097 MB free, and 6,873 MB available. That last number is the one to read: free memory plus cache the kernel can drop. A clean cached page, one identical to the copy on the disk, can be dropped the moment a program needs the frame. Linux fills idle RAM with cache on purpose, so memory the cache "uses" is still there when a program asks for it. Linux fills spare RAM with cache. Read available, not free.

Containers see the same thing. A container is a group of programs that the kernel runs apart from the rest of the machine. Its memory limit is kept in a cgroup, the kernel's record for a group of programs that it counts and limits together. The cgroup is charged for the page cache its programs bring in, next to their anonymous memory (memory that belongs to no file). The file memory.stat splits the two: writing a 512 MB file added 512 MB under file and nothing under anon. The container's memory use counts both, so a program that writes or reads big files can look close to its limit while holding little memory of its own. Before the OOM killer (the kernel's last resort, which ends a program to free memory) is called, the kernel drops clean file pages first.

Reads are the easy half, because a cached page that's lost can always be read again. Next, we'll see what happens to a write.

try.title: Read a file cold, then warm
steps: Start the lab box from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box. The lab box is a small Linux machine that runs in Docker (a program that runs separate small machines, called containers, on your computer), and your labs folder appears inside it as /labs.

os/c/l09/pcache.c counts how many pages of a file are in the page cache, with mincore, a system call that asks exactly that. With evict, it drops that one file's pages from the cache. It touches no other file, which matters in the Docker virtual machine that other containers share.
The block writes a 512 MB file with dd, evicts it, then reads it twice with cat. time prints how long each read took. Predict both real times, and what memory.stat does after the write.
Run it in the lab box. It deletes the file at the end.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/pcache os/c/l09/pcache.c grep -E '^(anon|file) ' /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.stat dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/segment.log bs=1M count=512 status=none grep -E '^(anon|file) ' /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.stat /tmp/pcache /tmp/segment.log evict time cat /tmp/segment.log > /dev/null /tmp/pcache /tmp/segment.log time cat /tmp/segment.log > /dev/null free -m rm /tmp/segment.log

try.expect:
The times depend on how busy the virtual machine is (another run took 1.0 s and 0.16 s):

file 28450816
anon 397312
file 565391360

real	0m3.313s

Writing the file added 512 MB to the container's file count and nothing to anon: the written pages are page cache. After evict, none of it was cached, and the first cat waited for the disk. That read put all 131,072 pages back in the cache, and the second cat was all sys time, the kernel copying from RAM. (real is the time on the clock, user the time in the program's own code, and sys the time in the kernel.) free -m is the whole virtual machine's view, and available is what programs could still get. On a Linux machine of your own, fincore, from the util-linux set of standard tools, does what pcache does.

sections.h: Writeback: a write lands in RAM, and the disk gets it later
sections.html:
dd, a command that copies data into a file, writes 64 MB to a file in /tmp in a fraction of a second. Right after, the container's memory.stat shows file_dirty 67108864: 64 MB that's in RAM and not on the disk.

write() doesn't wait for storage. It copies the program's bytes into page cache pages, marks each page dirty, meaning newer than the copy on the disk, and returns. Waiting for the disk on every call would make every small write pay for a trip to the device. And many writes never need to reach the disk one by one. A page rewritten a hundred times in a second can be written once, and pages written in order can go out as one large request.

A post office works the same way. You hand the clerk a letter, the clerk says "done" and drops it in the outgoing tray, and a van empties the tray now and then. Anyone who asks for your letter before the van comes gets it from the tray. In kernel terms, the tray is the page cache, a letter in it is a dirty page, and the van is writeback.

The van is the kernel's flusher threads, lines of work inside the kernel that write dirty pages to the disk later. This is writeback, and four things start it (the settings count time in centiseconds, hundredths of a second):

  • A page that has been dirty longer than vm.dirty_expire_centisecs (3000, so 30 s) is written at the flusher's next wake-up. The flusher wakes every vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs: 500 (5 s) by default, and 1500 (15 s) in the lab box's virtual machine (a computer simulated in software, which Docker runs).
  • When dirty data passes vm.dirty_background_ratio (10%) of the memory the kernel could use for it, the flusher starts writing in the background without waiting for age. In this virtual machine, that line sat between 390 and 690 MB, depending on how much memory was free.
  • Past vm.dirty_ratio (20%), a program that writes more is made to wait and help with the writing. That's when write() suddenly gets slow.
  • A program asks: fsync for one file, or sync for everything.

The stepper follows one log file through writes, writeback, fsync and a power cut.

Until writeback happens, the newest data exists only in RAM. Programs that read the file see it, because they read the page cache. If the machine loses power, it's gone, although every write() returned success. Here the post office picture breaks: a tray of letters survives a power cut, and RAM doesn't. If only the program dies, say from kill -9 (which ends a program at once), nothing is lost. The dirty pages belong to the kernel, not to the program, and they still go to the disk.

In the shared Docker virtual machine, the timing is noisy. In the runs for this lesson, 64 MB of dirty data waited 30 to 34 s when nothing else happened. It was written after anywhere from 0.2 to 20 s when another container called sync or pushed the machine past its background line. On a quiet Linux machine of your own, you'd see the 30 s rule every time.

Half a minute in RAM is fine for most files. It isn't fine for a payment that has just been approved. Next, we'll make a write wait for the disk, and see what that costs.

3000
1500
nr_dirty_threshold 326762
nr_dirty_background_threshold 163181
0 s: file_dirty 67108864

The first two lines are the rules: pages expire after 3000 centiseconds (30 s), and the flusher wakes every 1500 (15 s). The limits count pages across the whole virtual machine. Background writeback starts at 163,181 dirty pages (about 640 MB), and writers get slowed down at 326,762 (about 1.3 GB). In this run, most of the 64 MB went out at the 15 s mark, early, because writeback was already running for other containers' data. The last 8 MB waited until it was 30 s old. In quiet runs, all 64 MB stayed dirty until 30 to 34 s; in busy ones, it was gone within seconds. Until the count reaches 0, a power cut loses whatever is still dirty.

sections.h: fsync: waiting until the disk has the data, and why that's slow
sections.html:
ForceCost is a short Java program that adds 4 KB records to a log file, the way the payments program records each payment. A plain write() costs 7 to 14 µs (millionths of a second) a record. Calling FileChannel.force, Java's way of asking for fsync, after every record costs 2 to 9 ms a record in the lab box, several hundred times more. Forcing once per 100 records brings it down to tens of microseconds a record.

fsync(fd) is the system call that closes the gap between written and stored. (fd is the file descriptor, the number the kernel gave the program when it opened the file.) The kernel writes the file's dirty pages and its metadata, the facts about the file: its size, which blocks (pieces) of the disk hold the data, and its timestamps. Then it tells the device to flush its own write cache, a little memory inside the disk itself. It returns only when the device says the data is stored. Most of the time goes on that round trip, so it depends on the hardware. It's a few milliseconds in this virtual machine on a Mac. On servers, it's anywhere from tens of microseconds, for a fast SSD (NVMe) with power-loss protection (a small reserve of power that lets it save its cache if the power fails), to a millisecond or more for a disk reached over the network.

There's a lighter version. fdatasync skips metadata that isn't needed to read the data back, such as the time the file last changed. In Java, FileChannel.force(false) asks for the content only, which on Linux is fdatasync, and force(true) is fsync. And close() doesn't write anything to the disk on a local file system.

A program that must not lose a record it has confirmed has to fsync before it answers. Done for every record, one thread manages a few hundred records a second here. The way out is group commit. Collect the records that arrive while one fsync is running, write them all, fsync once, then answer every caller in the group. Each caller waits a little longer, and throughput (records per second) grows with the batch. At the post office, it's sending a whole bag of letters with each van instead of one.

Databases work this way. PostgreSQL, a popular database program, writes every change to its write-ahead log (a log where each change goes before anything else). A transaction is a group of changes that must happen together. PostgreSQL flushes its log when a transaction commits, the moment the database promises the changes are saved, and commits that arrive together can share one flush. Oracle, another database, reports the time a program spends waiting for that flush at commit as log file sync.

Kafka chose differently, on purpose. Its design document says a write to the log only means the data "is transferred into the kernel's pagecache", and by default a Kafka server doesn't fsync each message. A message survives because it sits in the page cache of several servers at once (the settings acks=all and min.insync.replicas make sure of that). It's a bet that they won't all lose power in the same second.

One more trap: if writeback fails, for example on a disk error, fsync reports the error once. In 2018, PostgreSQL's developers found that retrying fsync after a failure could succeed although the data was lost, because the kernel had already marked the pages clean. Since then, PostgreSQL treats a failed fsync as fatal, and recovers from its log. A write that matters isn't saved until fsync returns. Batch, so one fsync serves many.

fsync makes one file's data safe. Replacing a whole file has one more way to fail, and that's next.

try.title: Price a force per record against a force per batch

Predict the cost per record of each mode, and which system call force(false) makes. Then run it in the lab box.

write only             20000        259            13.0
force every record      1000       3201          3201.4
force every 100        20000       1592            79.6
strace: Process 59 attached
...

100.00    0.273127         227      1200           fdatasync

A force per record costs about 250 times as much as a write. Batching by 100 divides the force's cost by 100. strace counts 1,200 fdatasync calls (1,000 plus 20,000 / 100) and no fsync: force(false) is fdatasync. Its usecs/call column is the CPU time spent in the kernel, not the time spent waiting for the device, which is why it's far below the 3 ms per force.

sections.h: Replacing a file safely: write a copy, fsync it, rename it, fsync the folder
sections.html:
SafeWrite replaces routing.json, a small settings file that tells the payments program which bank to ask and how long to wait. It does it with five system calls. It creates a temporary file, writes it, fsyncs it, renames it over the old name, and fsyncs the directory, the folder that holds the file's name. Each call closes a different way a crash could leave a broken file.

The tempting way is to overwrite in place: open the file with O_TRUNC, which empties it, write the new content, and close it. Now picture a power cut after the emptying and before writeback. It leaves an empty file, or one of the right length full of zeros, and the old content is gone as well. ext4 is the usual Linux file system, the part of the kernel that arranges files on a disk. Its documentation calls the empty result the zero-length problem, and it even carries a workaround for programs that skip fsync. Even with an fsync at the end, there's a window between the emptying and the fsync when the disk holds neither version.

So never touch the old file. Write the new content to routing.json.tmp, then rename() it to routing.json. Rename replaces the name in one step: its manual page, rename(2), promises that no other program ever finds the name missing. A program reading the file opens either the old one or the new one. A change that happens all at once, or not at all, is called atomic.

That's atomic for running programs, but not yet for a crash. The rename is a change to the directory. POSIX is the standard that says how Unix systems such as Linux must behave, and nothing in it makes the rename reach the disk after the temporary file's data. ext4 keeps a journal, a log of its own changes to names and sizes, and commits it every 5 seconds, while data waits up to 30 s for writeback. It even has a special case (auto_da_alloc) for this pattern, because so many programs got it wrong. Other file systems and settings promise nothing. Without care, a power cut can leave the name pointing at a file whose bytes never arrived. Hence the fsync of the temporary file before the rename: the name can then only ever point at data that's already on the disk.

The last call is about durability, the promise that a saved change stays saved. After rename, the new name exists only in the cached copy of the directory. The fsync(2) manual says that an fsync of a file doesn't make sure its entry in the directory is on the disk. For that, you fsync the directory itself. Skip it, and a crash can bring back the old file, whole but out of date, after you told the caller the update was saved. To replace a file, never touch the old one. Write a copy, fsync it, rename it, fsync the directory.

In Java, that's FileChannel.force(true) on the temporary file, then Files.move(tmp, target, ATOMIC_MOVE), then opening the directory with FileChannel.open(dir, READ) and calling force(true) on that. Opening a directory as a channel works on Linux. The lab makes you prove the whole pattern: its tests cut the power after every single step.

The pattern works because a file's name and the file itself are two separate things on the disk. Why that is, and what else follows from it, is the next lesson's subject.

try.title: Trace a safe replace
steps: SafeWrite replaces /tmp/cfg/routing.json with the four steps of this section, and prints the result.

Before you run it, write down the system calls you expect, in order. Then run it in the lab box under strace, a tool that prints every system call a program makes. The grep keeps the lines for the settings folder, the forces and the rename.

Thread IDs, the numbers at the start of each line, differ between runs:

{"issuer": "acme-bank", "timeoutMs": 120}
37    openat(AT_FDCWD, "/tmp/cfg/routing.json.tmp", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0666) = 4
37    write(4, "{\"issuer\": \"acme-bank\", \"timeout"..., 42) = 42
37    fsync(4)                          = 0
37    renameat(AT_FDCWD, "/tmp/cfg/routing.json.tmp", AT_FDCWD, "/tmp/cfg/routing.json") = 0

The four steps, in order: write the temporary file, fsync it, renameat it over the old name, then open the directory itself and fsync it. (openat and renameat are the kernel's names for open and rename.) Files.move with ATOMIC_MOVE is a single renameat. The last openat is the program reading the file back to print it.

refs.title: ext4 mount options: commit and auto_da_alloc
OSTEP chapter 39: Files and Directories (fsync, rename)

opening:
Picture a power cut on the café's street. It comes two seconds after a customer taps their card. The card reader had already beeped. The payments program had written the payment to its log file and said "approved". When the power comes back, the payment isn't in the file.

Every step had reported success. The program asked to write, the computer said done, and reading the file straight after would have shown the new line. So it's easy to think a write that succeeded is on the disk. Everything a program can see agrees.

In Memory allocation, we followed the memory that programs ask for. The kernel also fills RAM on its own, with copies of files. In this lesson, we'll follow a read and a write into the kernel, watch a write wait half a minute for the disk, price the call that makes it wait, and replace a file so that a crash can't break it. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a payment approved two seconds before a power cut, and gone after it. write() had only put it in the page cache. fsync would have waited the few milliseconds for the disk, and group commit lets many payments share that wait.

On a Linux machine you can reach, grep -E 'Dirty|Writeback' /proc/meminfo shows how much written data is still only in RAM. Run it right after copying a big file, and again half a minute later.

Next, we'll take a file apart, and find out why deleting one doesn't always free its space.

compare.title: Overwriting in place against replacing by rename

a.label: Overwrite in place
a.title: a crash anywhere before fsync returns can leave neither version
a.html: int fd = open("routing.json", O_WRONLY | O_TRUNC); // the old content is gone from here on write(fd, buf, len); // the new content is only in the page cache fsync(fd); // until this returns: empty, zeros or old bytes close(fd);

b.label: Replace by rename
b.title: a crash anywhere leaves the old file or the new one
b.html: int fd = open("routing.json.tmp", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644); write(fd, buf, len); fsync(fd); // the new bytes are on disk close(fd); rename("routing.json.tmp", "routing.json"); // the switch: one directory entry changes int dir = open(".", O_RDONLY); fsync(dir); // the switch is on disk too close(dir);

compare.note: Both versions write the same bytes, and both call fsync. The difference is what's on the disk at every moment in between. On the left, the first line destroys the old file, and the new one is complete only after the third. On the right, the old file is untouched until a single rename swaps the name, and the new file's data is already on the disk when it does. The right side costs one more fsync, on the directory, and a file name for the temporary copy.

worked.title: Write the nightly payouts file so that a crash can't break it, in Kotlin

steps.say: The nightly payouts file lists what each shop is owed for the day. Banks call it a settlement file, and so does the code. Write the whole file under a temporary name in the same directory as the real one: rename works only within one file system, so /tmp won't do. Loop on write, since a channel may write less than the whole buffer, then force the content and metadata.
steps.code: val tmp = target.resolveSibling("${target.fileName}.tmp") FileChannel.open(tmp, StandardOpenOption.CREATE, StandardOpenOption.TRUNCATE_EXISTING, StandardOpenOption.WRITE).use { ch -> val buf = ByteBuffer.wrap(csv.toByteArray()) while (buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(buf) ch.force(true) // fsync: the bytes are on disk before any name points at them }

steps.say: Swap the name. ATOMIC_MOVE makes Files.move a single rename(2), or makes it fail with AtomicMoveNotSupportedException instead of quietly copying and deleting.
steps.code: Files.move(tmp, target, StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE) // readers see the old file or the new one

steps.say: Make the rename itself durable by forcing the directory. On Linux, a directory opens as a read-only channel.
steps.code: FileChannel.open(target.parent, StandardOpenOption.READ).use { it.force(true) } // fsync of the directory

steps.say: Only now report the file as ready. Check the order once under strace; it should match the SafeWrite trace from this lesson.
steps.code: strace -f -o /tmp/export.txt -e trace=openat,write,fsync,renameat java ... grep -E 'settlement|fsync|renameat' /tmp/export.txt # the order to look for, as in the SafeWrite trace: # openat(tmp, O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC), write, fsync(tmp), renameat(tmp, target), openat(dir, O_RDONLY), fsync(dir)

lab.title: Build a page cache that can lose your data, then make it safe
steps: Read PageCache.kt. Disk is what survives a crash. Kernel holds the page cache, a clock, a journal that saves names and sizes every 5 s, and crash(). create, read, truncate, rename, fsyncDir, commitMetadata and writeBackAll are written for you, and so is Config.overwrite, the unsafe way.
Run the tests from the labs folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All eleven fail for now.
Write write: copy the bytes into cached pages, mark them dirty, note when each page went from clean to dirty, and grow the file's size.
Write fsync for one file only, then tick. The journal commits at every multiple of commitMs, and the flusher writes back pages dirty for at least expireMs at every multiple of wakeMs.
Write Config.replace in four calls. Then read the two crash tests: they cut the power after every step, with four different things the kernel might have written just before.
hints: A write can cross page boundaries: walk it with index = at / Disk.PAGE and inPage = at % Disk.PAGE, copying minOf(Disk.PAGE - inPage, remaining) bytes each time.
Set dirtiedAt only when a page goes from clean to dirty. Otherwise a page rewritten every second would never get old enough to write back.
In tick, jump the clock straight to the next multiple of commitMs or wakeMs with (now / step + 1) * step, rather than counting milliseconds.
If the crash test fails on the step after rename, check that the fsync of the temporary file came before the rename.

drill.title: Size a group commit
drill.prompt: A log of changes to the shops' balances must force every record to the disk before the caller gets an answer. One force takes 2 ms, and writing a record into the page cache costs almost nothing. Callers arrive at 5,000 records a second. Write Kotlin that prints the throughput of one force per record, the smallest batch that keeps up with 5,000 a second, and the longest a caller then waits.

answer.html: val forceMs = 2.0 val arrivalsPerSec = 5_000 val perRecord = 1_000 / forceMs // 500 records/s: one force each val forcesPerSec = 1_000 / forceMs // 500 forces a second at most val batch = Math.ceil(arrivalsPerSec / forcesPerSec).toInt() // 10 records per force // worst case: arrive just as a force starts, wait for it (2 ms), then for your own batch's force (2 ms) val worstWaitMs = 2 * forceMs // about 4 ms println("$perRecord/s per record, batch of $batch, worst wait $worstWaitMs ms")

recap: Every file read and write goes through the page cache, one shared copy of file pages in RAM. A miss reads from storage, and a hit only copies. mmap of a file maps the same pages.
available, not free, is the memory programs can still get, because clean cache pages are dropped on demand. In a container, cache counts as file, next to anon.
write() copies into the cache, marks pages dirty and returns. The flusher writes them about 30 s later, sooner past dirty_background_ratio, and writers are slowed down past dirty_ratio.

A power cut loses dirty pages; a crashed program doesn't. fsync (Java's force(true)) or fdatasync (force(false)) writes one file's pages and waits for the device. That takes milliseconds, so batch records with group commit.

To replace a file: write a temporary file, fsync it, rename it over the target, fsync the directory. A crash then leaves the old file or the new one, and the new one for sure once the last step returns.
The limit: all of this protects data on one machine's disk. If that disk dies, the data goes with it however carefully it was written, which is why databases also keep copies on other machines.

explain.prompt: A friend says: "Our program writes the nightly payouts file with write() and close(), and the disk's file system keeps a journal, so the file is safe once the method returns." Explain what can go wrong, and what the method should do instead.
explain.answer: When write() returns, the bytes are only in the page cache: dirty pages in RAM that the kernel writes to the disk about 30 seconds later, or sooner if memory runs short. close() doesn't change that. If the program crashes, the kernel still writes the pages, so tests never show a problem. But if the machine loses power, or the kernel itself crashes, in that window, the data is gone, though every call succeeded. The journal doesn't help. ext4's journal is a log of the file system's own changes to names and sizes, kept so the file system stays in order. It can save the new file's size or name before the data, so after a crash we could find an empty file, or one full of zeros, under the real name. The method should write the file under a temporary name in the same directory, and call force(true) on it so the data is on the disk. Then it should Files.move it over the real name with ATOMIC_MOVE, and force the directory so the rename itself is safe. After a crash, the bank then sees either the previous file or the complete new one, and once the method returns, the new one for sure. It costs a couple of trips to the device, a few milliseconds, once per file.

deeper.html:
On a Linux machine of your own, you can watch the page cache without the care this lesson takes in the shared Docker virtual machine. sync; echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches writes back everything and then drops every clean cached page on the machine, so the next read of any file is cold. fincore FILE (from util-linux) prints how much of a file is cached, and grep -E 'Dirty|Writeback' /proc/meminfo shows the machine's dirty and in-flight totals. Don't drop caches on a shared machine, or on one that serves real users: every program pays for the cold reads afterwards.

Some programs skip the page cache. Opening a file with O_DIRECT makes reads and writes go straight between the program's buffer and the device, with rules about how buffers and positions line up. Databases that keep their own cache of pages, such as Oracle and MySQL's InnoDB in common setups, use it so pages aren't cached twice. O_DIRECT alone still isn't durable: the device has a write cache too, so the database still calls fsync or fdatasync at commit.

The fsync error story is worth reading in full in LWN's "PostgreSQL's fsync() surprise" (2018). When writeback of a page fails, the kernel reports the error to the next fsync on that file, and may then treat the page as clean. A program that logs the error and retries can get success while the data never reached the disk. Patches in kernel 4.13 improved how these errors reach programs, but a program that opens the file after the error can still miss it entirely, as the article explains. The lesson for programs didn't change: a failed fsync means data may be lost, and the only safe reaction is to stop and recover from something you know is on the disk, which is what PostgreSQL does now.
